Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

lexsync (development version)

  • Design, schema and registry files are read as UTF-8 whatever the session’s character type. yaml::read_yaml() converted each file to the session’s encoding, so under the C locale, as in a container or a batch job without a UTF-8 locale, a file stopped at its first accented letter: config/design_es_lexdec.yaml read as an empty design, list_corpora() and fetch_corpus() failed on the bundled registry’s citations, and the datasheet left out a cached corpus’s citation without a word. A file that is not UTF-8 is now refused, as the Python engine refuses it, where it used to be cut short with a warning, and a literal block scalar that ends a file keeps its final line break, as it does in Python.

  • The hash keys behind the trial order, list balancing, jitter and the tie-break between candidates are UTF-8 in every locale. Under the C locale, paste() turned a latin1-marked condition label into escape text and enc2utf8() did the same to an unmarked one, so such labels ranked by other digests than in the Python engine. The 0.1.0 entry below that says a latin1-marked label “can no longer rank by different digests” held in a UTF-8 session only. A run under the C locale now writes the stimuli, reports and experiments of the Spanish and Chinese demonstrations byte for byte.

  • list_corpora() and fetch_corpus() refuse a registry_path that does not exist with lexsync’s own message, not the connection error file() gave. The Python twin read whichever registry its search found next.

  • resample_stimuli() and validate_design() refuse a resample.n_sets that is not a whole number of at least 1, the rule n_per_condition follows. A fractional count was truncated in silence, a logical or a quoted number was taken as a count, and zero gave an empty selection.

  • describe_stimuli() refuses a dimension or a grouping column the stimuli do not carry, and so do match_report() and match_report_continuous(), which are built on it. A misspelt dimension gave a table of missing values with an n of 0, which looked complete. The pipeline reports only the columns it has, so no run is affected.

  • The licence notice for the bundled CC BY-SA lexica is installed with the package, as COPYRIGHTS. R does not install LICENSE.note, which the Copyright field named, so binary installations carried the lexica without it. LICENSE.note now points to inst/COPYRIGHTS, and the Copyright field, the citation footer and the About guide name the installed file.

  • The spelling test fails a check run with NOT_CRAN set, as in devtools::check() and on GitHub Actions, when the help pages, the vignettes, the README, this file or the package description use a word found neither in the British English dictionary nor in inst/WORDLIST. It used to list such words and carry on, so a misspelling left only a NOTE, which does not fail a run. CRAN and a plain R CMD check still skip the test. The documentation has no such word today, so the word list is unchanged.

  • The datasheet records the materials source, the stimuli file and every artefact with forward slashes, as the Python engine does. A run given Windows paths recorded them with backslashes.

  • The apps’ download bundles reproduce their own record. The apps ran a temporary copy of the design with absolute paths and then bundled the displayed design, so the bundled datasheet’s design checksum matched no file in the bundle, and the datasheet and run logs exposed the user’s home and temporary directories. They now run the exported command in a folder laid out like the bundle, and the Download tab archives that folder, with the outputs under output/. Rerunning the exported code in the unzipped folder rewrites them with the same bytes, run logs apart. The PsychoPy and OpenSesame downloads are zip archives holding the tables those experiments load, and each app removes a run’s folder once its results leave the screen.

  • The Shiny app’s presets set the matched dimensions and the matching method, as the Streamlit app’s presets do. Its neighbourhood preset matched on N, the dimension it manipulates, and on OLD20, a close correlate of N, and it left length unmatched. Both apps now warn when ‘Match on’ names a dimension whose windows differ between conditions, and neither runs a factorial design with nothing to match on. Their command lines quote the design file’s name and run in cmd.exe and Windows PowerShell, and the Streamlit app’s R line now passes the outdir that run_pipeline() requires. The interval column is labelled by the configured alpha, and the sentence under the exported code says that the engines agree byte for byte only when the run’s datasheet says so. The Shiny method selector carries the Streamlit app’s note on mahalanobis and optimal. Both apps open on en_v2, the English lexicon screened against SUBTLEX-US, and keep only its unmarked forms unless ‘Screened forms only’ is cleared, as the shipped English designs do. A session left at its defaults therefore selects different words from before. The Streamlit app no longer passes use_container_width, an argument Streamlit is removing, and needs Streamlit 1.49 or later.

  • counterbalance.max_run caps runs of one condition, or of one value of any column named in counterbalance.run_on, in the trial order. counterbalance() repairs the seeded order deterministically, taking at each step the earliest trial in it that keeps the limit and leaves the rest of the list able to keep it, so it refuses only a limit no order can meet, with a message giving the counts. A missing value counts as a value of its own. With fillers, the limit applies to the order they are interleaved in, and the practice trials keep it on their own. The datasheet records the limit and the longest run realised in each presentation version as counterbalancing$max_run, a field of datasheet format 1.2, and the Methods text states it, citing van Casteren and Davis (2006). The shipped designs hold runs of up to eleven trials of one condition, and the lexical decisions up to seven consecutive trials with the same correct key. Both new keys are off by default, so no shipped design changes.

  • counterbalance.orders: m gives each list m trial orders. counterbalance() adds order_1 to order_m, each trial’s position in each order, to the stimuli and the loop tables. Order 1 is the seeded order, and order j from 2 is ranked by the SHA-256 of seed|order<j>|replicate|list|set|condition. Participant p runs version ((p - 1) mod V) + 1 in order (((p - 1) div V) mod m) + 1: the PsychoPy script and the jsPsych page sort the version’s trials by that order and record it in every data row, and OpenSesame gets one experiment per version and order, <base>_list<k>_order<j>.osexp, whose start-up check compares the order too. Participants on one list no longer all meet the same order. The datasheet records counterbalancing$orders (the number of orders and the rule), a field of datasheet format 1.2.

  • Every generated PsychoPy script and jsPsych page carries ORDERS and the code that picks an order, so their bytes change, and so do the checksums the datasheets record of them and of the schema, whose comments describe the new keys. No stimulus, loop table or OpenSesame experiment moves.

  • The documentation said that practice trials are shuffled so that participants meet them in different orders. Every participant given a list meets them in one fixed order, as the design intends, and the text now says so.

  • counterbalance.scale: mad balances lists on each dimension’s deviations from its mean in units of its mean absolute deviation, so a dimension’s weight no longer depends on where its scale starts. The values are rounded to hundredths by the shared rounder before the integer mean and the unit are taken, so adding a constant that is a whole number of hundredths leaves the lists unchanged. The default, mean, divides by the dimension’s mean, which suits ratio scales only: Zipf frequency, whose scale starts near 3, carried the least weight of the four dimensions in en_balanced_lists, and re-expressing it as Zipf - 3 moved 22 of 40 sets to another list. The default is unchanged so running studies keep their lists. Under mad, the balance_lists() report and the datasheet’s counterbalancing$optimise record give scale, a field of datasheet format 1.2, cost_unit names the unit and the Methods paragraph names the scale. validate_design() refuses any other scale, and the key joins the design vocabulary in both engines, whose suites pin the new digest. The optimiser’s exact-integer guard now bounds the sum of the absolute set totals, since signed deviations can sum to near zero, and gives the same answer as before for values of one sign. The schema’s comments describe the option in all three copies. The edit changes config/schema.yaml, so every committed datasheet records a new schema digest and every run log a new datasheet checksum. The twin-edge cases scale_mad and scale_unknown pin both engines to one outcome.

  • normalise_lexicon() turns a delimited corpus file into a lexicon load_lexicon() reads. It applies a column map, reads tab-separated files, derives Zipf values from frequencies per million (Zipf = log10(per million) + 3) and writes word and freq_zipf, with freq_permillion and pos when the file has them. Words are lower-cased and put in NFC, and a form listed more than once keeps its first row or, under a registry entry’s duplicates: sum, the sum of its rows’ frequencies, as Lexique needs. A message counts the derived values that lay within 1e-9 of a rounding boundary, the one step at which the two engines’ log10() could round a value apart, and a run over a lexicon carrying freq_permillion records the count in its run log and as materials_source$zipf_derivation, a field of datasheet format 1.2. fetch_corpus("subtlex_us") downloads SUBTLEX-US from openlexicon, checks its SHA-256 and normalises it in either engine. No registered corpus could be fetched before. An entry may also name a derived file, a lexicon already normalised, which is fetched in its place. The registry header describes this route where it said that the column maps were not yet applied. Lexique 3.83 stays a listed entry: the manual confirms that it splits a homograph’s frequency between rows, so the entry records duplicates: sum, but the forms its film corpus never attests carry a frequency of 0, which has no Zipf value.

  • load_lexicon() refuses Zipf values outside 0 to 9, which are frequencies per million in the wrong column. A log count such as SUBTLEX-US’s Lg10WF lies inside that range and must still be converted.

  • fetch_corpus() refuses a corpus name containing a path before it reads the registry, so an edited registry cannot make it write outside the cache. Its refusals name the registry they read and say when an entry registers no download address, and a wordfreq language code now gets an explanation that its lexicon is built by the Python package (lexsync fetch fr) and read here with load_lexicon(), where the refusal said the language was not in the registry.

  • A masked_priming paradigm presents a forward mask of hash marks for 500 ms, a lower-case prime for three frames and an upper-case target that stays until the response, the procedure of Forster and Davis (1984). Without a forward mask, a prime this brief is usually visible. The target collects its response from its onset and stays on screen for the whole 2,000 ms window. A text event’s case: upper or case: lower is applied by the runners when they display it, with str.upper() and str.lower() in PsychoPy and OpenSesame and toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() in jsPsych, so the loop tables and the data files keep each item as it was written. lexsync does not change the case itself, because toupper() leaves the German sharp s unchanged where Python turns it into two letters. A mask’s length_of names the fields whose longest value sets its length. Its one character is repeated as many times as that value has characters, not bytes, counted over every trial when the experiments are written, so each target and each list shows the same mask. validate_design() refuses a case other than upper or lower and a case on any event but a text event. It also refuses length_of on any event but a mask and on a mask whose content is not one character. export_experiments() refuses a length_of field the trials do not have. The two keys join the design vocabulary in both engines, whose suites pin the new digest, and the schema’s comments describe them. The priming paradigm is unchanged and is documented as backward-masked, as is its label in the demos index. The registry is pinned by a digest that both suites compute, so a paradigm changed in one engine only fails both. Every demonstration’s experiments, datasheets and run logs change, because the PsychoPy and jsPsych templates do. The twin-edge case masked_priming_text pins both engines to one outcome.

  • The en_rastle_repro example uses masked priming with nonword targets, and en_andrews_repro gains pseudowords, so both run as lexical-decision tasks. en_rastle_repro interleaves twelve nonword targets, each with a word prime, as fillers (items/rastle_nonword_fillers_en.csv), and en_andrews_repro one pseudoword per selected word (items/andrews_pseudoword_fillers_en.csv). The nonwords were made once with the package’s letter-substitution generator and checked against wordfreq’s known English forms, and each design’s comment gives the command and lists what still differs from the original study. Each design puts its word conditions on the left arrow key, gives its fillers the right and shows its own instructions. Their stimuli files gain a block column and their trials are renumbered, since the fillers are interleaved with the words. The items, sets, lists and conditions are the same, and no descriptives or comparisons change.

  • Generated experiments show task instructions before the first trial and wait for the space bar, so the experimenter can start the run when the participant is ready. A design sets the text with instructions. It may hold line breaks and no other control character, and every target carries it as data. Without it, a lexical decision, a categorisation and a design with comprehension questions get English instructions that say what their keys mean. The run log notes a design in another language that gives no text of its own, and a design whose keys the instructions can only name, as in every factorial and priming demonstration. A lexical-decision design states its response mapping: word on the response event’s first key and pseudoword on its second, unless the design gives response_mapping, and rotate_mapping_by_list: true rotates the keys across lists. A mapping that names a key the response event does not allow, or leaves a condition’s trials without an answer, is refused. The loop tables carry each trial’s correct key in answer, so accuracy can be scored on every trial of a lexical decision, where it could be scored only on practice and filler trials. jsPsych records a key by the browser’s name for it, so the jsPsych page names each answer that way, arrowleft for left, as it already named the keys, and in every target a correct response equals its trial’s answer. export_experiments() derives the answers as it assigns the trigger codes, so the stimuli file does not change. A practice or filler table keeps its own answers, and the run log notes any that the mapping contradicts. The datasheet records the mapping as presentation$response_mapping, a field of datasheet format 1.2, and its Methods text says which key the participants pressed for which condition. The schema’s comments describe the three keys. Every demonstration’s experiments, datasheets and run logs change, and the loop tables of the three lexical decisions carry an answer on every trial. The twin-edge cases mapping_rotated and instructions_text pin both engines to one outcome. No design selects different items.

  • The lexical-decision practice table no longer presents the English word ‘plank’ as a pseudoword. Its replacement, ‘plang’, came from the package’s own generator and is not among wordfreq’s English forms, and design_en_lexdec_blocks.yaml records the command. The categorisation example adds 16 non-member foils as fillers (items/categorisation_foils_en.csv), nouns that do not belong to the category they appear under, so pressing the ‘yes’ key on every trial no longer scores perfectly. Each list now holds 16 ‘yes’ and 16 ‘no’ trials. The foils are interleaved with the members, so the example’s stimuli file gains a block column and its trials are renumbered, while the same items stay in the same lists and conditions.

  • The PsychoPy and jsPsych experiments paused wherever the block changed. Fillers are interleaved with the main trials so that nothing sets them apart, yet a pause came before and after every filler, and each pause after one said that the practice had ended. Fillers now run with the main trials, and the one pause comes where the practice trials end, in design_en_lexdec_blocks.yaml and in the categorisation example, whose foils are fillers.

  • CITATION.cff and codemeta.json, which describe the repository and so both packages, give the Zenodo concept DOI, which archives every GitHub release of both, in place of the DOI that CRAN assigned to the R package. They list each package’s identifiers, marked with the package they name. citation("lexsync") is unchanged and gives the CRAN DOI.

  • citation("lexsync") names its publisher in full, “Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN)”, where it said “CRAN”, and the About page’s reference and BibTeX entry and the R reference in codemeta.json now name it too. Every reference across the package family and the author’s website now names CRAN in the same words.

  • The CRAN DOI and the Zenodo DOI are shown as full links on the website and in the README. The README gains a badge for the DOI CRAN assigned, for GitHub and CRAN, which the home page leaves out of its sidebar, where the DOI is already given under Citation.

  • 28 of the committed datasheets recorded the SHA-256 of a copy of corpora/derived/en.csv or es.csv whose line endings one machine had converted to CRLF, so the digest could not be reproduced from a checkout and read as altered materials. Two of them also recorded such a copy of config/design_en_priming_continuous.yaml. The datasheets are regenerated from the committed bytes, and a test in both engines recomputes every recorded digest, the design and schema digests included. No stimulus, report table or experiment changes. The run logs of the 14 designs concerned change with their datasheets, whose MD5 they record.

  • Generated OpenSesame experiments no longer pass stimulus text through OpenSesame’s variable store, which evaluates it. In OpenSesame 4.x, a loop cell containing { runs as a Python f-string, and in 3.3 a leading = or [=...] runs Python, so an item table shared with a laboratory could execute code on the machine that presents it. Ordinary words in the English lexicon, such as ‘infinity’ and ‘nan’, could stop an OpenSesame 4.x session, though no demonstration design selected one. The loop table now holds only numbers: lexsync_row, the trial’s position in loop order, with lexsync_trial, lexsync_list, lexsync_set, the trigger codes, critical_region and any per-trial duration. The prefix stops the columns from shadowing Python’s built-in list and set in OpenSesame 4’s inline scripts. The inline scripts read the presented text, condition, block and answer from a companion file, <base>_opensesame_text.csv, to be copied with the experiment. export_opensesame() refuses a value in one of the numeric columns that is not a plain number, naming the column. A practice timeout is reported as ‘Too slow’. Both versions scored it as a wrong key, because the response came back as the string ‘None’. The 0.1.0 notes said stimulus text was always safe. That held for PsychoPy and jsPsych but not for OpenSesame. Every demonstration’s .osexp and OpenSesame loop table change, and each demonstration gains a text table. The datasheets and run logs change with them, since they record the experiment’s checksum. No stimulus moves.

  • The Shiny app writes an edit to the conditions table into the cell that was edited. Every edit landed one column to the left, because DT::editData() was called without rownames = FALSE, so a custom condition could not be entered. The bounds of the second factor, which the one-factor presets leave empty, are now numeric columns, so a bound typed there is kept as a number. They were logical columns, on which DT warned and stored the typed text.

  • The R engine no longer reads a design key by partial matching. R’s $ accepts the start of a name when no name matches in full, so a key that began another key’s name stood in for that key when it was absent. font_size: 40 set the font of all three generated experiments to ‘40’, language_tag served as language, and an annotation named continuous_notes made a factorial design fail. Design, schema and corpus-registry entries are now read by exact name, so a design carrying font_size or continuous_notes runs as it does in Python, and one that gives language_tag without language stops, as it does in Python. The Python engine was never affected.

  • Numbers in the Markdown datasheet and the Methods paragraph are formatted by lexsync itself, not by each language’s printf, which rounds decimal ties differently: R on Windows printed 0.0825 as 0.082 where Python printed 0.083. A displayed value is rounded half away from zero from the value the JSON record stores, so a statistic stored as 0.745 now shows as 0.75 in both engines, where both printed 0.74. Some two-place cells in the committed datasheets of 10 designs change for this reason, and the Methods paragraph of es_freqcontrast now gives the interval as [-0.19, 0.34]. A cell in which the R datasheet of en_andrews_repro disagreed with Python’s (-0.46 against -0.47) now agrees. The TOST p column is printed to four places in both engines, and a p that rounds to zero is shown as < 0.0001. R wrote such a column as 9e-04 and 1, Python as 0.0009 and 1.0. No JSON record, stimulus, report table or experiment changes. The run logs of the 10 designs change with their datasheets, whose MD5 they record.

  • Both engines read CSV input by one rule. Header names and fields are trimmed, and an empty field or NA is missing. A column is numeric only when every value is a plain decimal number (no thousands separators), logical only when every value is TRUE or FALSE (in upper, lower or title case), and text otherwise. The Python engine did not trim, so a padded category or header made it refuse a design the R engine ran. The R engine guessed types from the first 1,000 rows and read T and F as logical, 1,000 as a number and ISO dates as dates, so a pass-through column could be written F by one engine and FALSE by the other. A header that names a column twice is now refused, an empty header cell is named by its position (...3), and load_lexicon() refuses a frequency column that is not numeric, naming the first value that is not a plain number. The R engine parses every plain decimal number to the nearest double, as Python’s float() does, because readr’s parser could miss it by one unit in the last place (50.768212762897100, for instance). A number of up to 15 significant digits, with a power of ten within 10^22, takes one exact operation, and any other is rounded in exact integer arithmetic, because as.numeric() misses as well, now and then on x86-64 and far more often on Apple Silicon, where R CMD check read 0.12345678901234567 one unit away. R wrote a negative zero as -0 and Python as 0, so both engines now read it as zero. Every demonstration’s stimuli and reports are unchanged.

  • Changes list assignment: a paradigm’s Latin-square recipe now applies when a design lists its own events. Any events: list made counterbalance() deal the items factorially, so a priming, categorisation or self-paced reading design with per-trial timing showed every target in both conditions of each list (in en_priming_jitter, six targets per list, each twice), while the datasheet and the Methods text described a Latin square. counterbalance.recipe (factorial or latin_square_target) overrides the paradigm’s recipe, and counterbalance.optimise is now refused for these designs, as for every Latin-square design. Of the shipped examples only en_priming_jitter moves: each of its two lists now shows all twelve targets once, and its stimuli, experiments and datasheets are regenerated.

  • The datasheet, now format 1.2, records the counterbalancing that ran. It takes the recipe from the resolver that counterbalance() dispatches on, and no longer infers it from the item source, which recorded a table-sourced lexical-decision design as a Latin square. It records the lists the counterbalancing realised, in place of counterbalance.lists with a default of 1, and gives per-list cell counts. An incomplete Latin-square rotation (a single list, or lists or item sets not a multiple of the number of conditions) is reported in the run log and the datasheet and described as incomplete in the Methods text, and counterbalance.incomplete: error, in the design or the schema, refuses it. A factorial design asking for more lists than item sets is refused, because the surplus lists would be empty. Every committed datasheet and run log is regenerated, and no other stimulus moves.

  • The en_priming_jitter example names its per-trial column prime_ms. It was called soa_ms, but a 33 ms mask follows the prime, so the stimulus-onset asynchrony is prime_ms plus 33 ms.

  • Designs are checked before anything is selected or written, by the new validate_design(), which run_pipeline() calls right after reading the design and the schema. A key one edit from a known key of up to five characters, or two edits from a longer one, is refused as a probable typo and named with the key it was probably meant to be (n_per_conditon silently gave the default 20 items). Any other unknown key is reported in the run log and will be refused in a later release, so annotations belong in description or a key beginning x_. A missing or non-text name or language, an unsafe name or font, a bad trigger address or response key, a non-text or repeated condition name and a missing or empty match_on are refused with one message in both engines. They used to fail at export, after four files had been written, or at different points in each engine, and without match_on this engine paired the alphabetically first words.

  • The R engine reads an unquoted y or n in a design as text, as the Python engine does. It read them as TRUE and FALSE, so keys: [y, n] generated experiments that waited for keys named TRUE and FALSE, which no participant can press. A YAML boolean given as a response key (an unquoted yes, no, on or off) is refused with a hint to quote it, and validate_design() refuses a counterbalance.optimise that is not true or false, since optimise: n or 1 balanced the lists in the Python engine only. The twin-edge cases yn_keys, yes_no_keys, optimise_n and language_no pin both engines to these outcomes.

  • A norms entry’s join key is written join_on:. Both engines’ YAML readers took the documented on: for the boolean true, so every join silently used word. A bare on: is now read as the join key, with a note in the run log, and any other key in a norms entry is refused, so a misspelt join_on no longer falls back to word. An entry that is not a mapping, such as a bare file name, is refused as needing a path, where it used to stop the run with R’s own error. This engine also joined each entry of a norms: block written as a mapping of named entries, such as conc: {path: norms.csv}, which the Python engine refused. Both engines now refuse it and name conc as an unknown key. The datasheet still records the key as on. The schema’s comment now shows join_on:. The 42 committed datasheets record the schema’s SHA-256 and the run logs record each datasheet’s MD5, so both are regenerated. No stimulus, report table or experiment changes. The twin-edge case norms_on_bare pins the join on lemma.

  • n_per_condition is resolved by one rule everywhere. A whole number written as 4.0 is accepted, and 0 is refused by match_stimuli() and select_continuous_stimuli(), which failed here with an obscure error and returned their default size in Python. A null tolerance is read as modifyList() reads it in both engines, and a schema without a matching: block works in Python.

  • A design whose name or language has non-ASCII characters writes its files under a stem with an eight-character checksum suffix, given by the new design_stem(), so two designs with Chinese names in the same language no longer overwrite each other’s files and an all-Chinese name no longer gives files whose names begin with a dot or underscore. run_all() refuses two designs that would write the same files, such as en-lexdec and en_lexdec.

  • The schema gains comments on the key check and on a null tolerance, so the 42 committed datasheets, which record its SHA-256, and the run logs, which record the datasheets’ MD5, are regenerated. No stimulus, report table or experiment changes.

  • Both engines normalise text keys to Unicode NFC. Lexicon and pool words and norm-table and pair-member keys are normalised after the trimming and case-folding they already received. The item id, condition and presented fields of an item table, practice and filler tables included, and a reference_words list passed to run_pipeline() are normalised as read. The two encodings of an accented letter, precomposed or with a combining accent, used to make two words of one. Both could then be selected, into opposite conditions of one matched set and with different lengths, and a norm or member join missed whichever spelling the lexicon did not use. De-duplication keeps the first row in file order. When normalisation rewrites or merges any form, the run log says how many, and the datasheet records the counts as materials_source$input_normalisation, a field of datasheet format 1.2. Every demonstration’s output is unchanged, and the twin-edge case nfd_pool pins the new outcome.

  • Matching excludes candidates that lack a matched dimension, in every method and before anything is selected, and the run log and the datasheet record how many each condition lost (selection.incomplete_dropped, a 1.2 field present only when a condition lost any). An anchor item missing a matched value used to be paired with the alphabetically first candidate in its window, or to re-pick a used candidate and stop the run with a false ‘overlapping conditions’ error. joint filled a shortfall with incomplete pairs, optimal failed with a solver error that differed between the engines, and select_continuous_stimuli() selected items without the predictor (4 of 10 when 40% of the pool lacked it). The documentation already promised the exclusion. The shortfall policy applies to what remains, a condition left without a complete candidate is refused by name, and a word repeated within one condition, which used to be reported as overlapping conditions, is reported as an internal error. The datasheet’s verdict on whether the pairwise cap fired, and the Methods text’s count of eligible candidates, leave the excluded candidates out. For a design whose pool has such candidates the selection changes, a breaking change under the package’s versioning rule. No shipped design has one, so no stimulus, report table or experiment moves. The schema’s note on norm coverage, corrected in all three copies, changes config/schema.yaml, so every committed datasheet records a new schema digest and every run log a new datasheet checksum.

  • resample_stimuli() records the candidates its first replicate excluded for a missing matched value, those of the whole pool, so the run log and the datasheet of a resampled design report them as well. Its "audit" attribute had been that of the first replicate in R, and in Python it was present only when all the replicates held the same one. A selection no longer passes on an audit its pool already carried. The Python engine did so whatever the method, and the R engine in select_continuous_stimuli().

  • mahalanobis matching estimates the correlations from the rows complete on the matched dimensions, and refuses a pool with fewer than k + 2 of them for k dimensions. A dimension with any missing value used to lose all its correlations and enter the distance as an independent term.

  • Joint matching on a dimension with missing values over more than 1,200 candidates failed in R (‘missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed’) and ran in Python. .exact_sum() now returns NA for such input, as the Python engine’s sum returns NaN. It also returns NaN where opposite infinities make the running sum NaN, a case in which it stopped in the same way.

  • Generated experiments present one counterbalancing version to each participant. The PsychoPy, OpenSesame and jsPsych experiments used to present every list in one session, interleaved, so in a Latin-square design each target appeared in both conditions (in en_priming, all 12 targets twice, three of them on consecutive trials), and in a resampled design every participant saw all the replicates. The 0.1.0 notes said that a categorisation participant never sees the same target twice. That held within a list only. A version is one (replicate, list) pair of the presented trials, numbered from 1 in that order, and participant p runs version ((p - 1) mod V) + 1 of V, the rule participant_table() uses. The PsychoPy script reads --participant and --version, or --list without replicates, from its command line. Launched with neither, it asks for them in a dialogue, which a design with one version also shows and runs on blank answers. It stops on a version it does not have. The jsPsych page reads ?participant=, ?version= or ?list= from its address, and a page with several versions opened without one says how to open it and runs nothing. Every page names its data file after the participant and the version, so a page with one version saves <title>_v1.csv. The OpenSesame target writes one experiment per version (<base>_list<k>.osexp, or <base>_rep<r>_list<k>.osexp with replicates), each with its own tables, and each warns when the subject number belongs to another version. A design with one list and no replicates keeps its file names. export_experiments() lists every file it wrote as files, beside the three paths it returned before, so unlist() of its result now holds each script twice. The exporters refuse a list or replicate value that is not a whole number, read by one rule in both engines, since the versions are numbered by those values. In a resampled design with practice or filler trials, each version has its own copy of them, and fillers no longer stop such a design with an error about a missing hash-key component. The loop tables carry replicate and keep each version’s trials together. The datasheet records counterbalancing.versions and counterbalancing.assignment, and its Methods text says that each participant was presented one version. Its artefact list and the run log include the loop and text tables, which hold the trial order and the trigger codes. Every demonstration’s experiments, datasheets and run logs change, and the seven multi-list designs and en_resample have one OpenSesame experiment per version in place of <base>.osexp. No stimulus changes.

  • A design can refer to a derived dimension (n_density, old20, bigram_freq) in a condition’s define_by, in pool_filters, as a continuous predictor or control, or in counterbalance.balance_on, as well as in match_on. When the lexicon lacks the dimension, run_pipeline() computes it against the lexicon, after the filters the lexicon can answer and before those on the derived dimension. A high- against low-bigram contrast, a continuous design with bigram_freq as its predictor, or an N design on a lexicon built by lexsync fetch used to fail with ‘absent from the pool’. Two twin-edge cases, bigram_contrast and fetched_es_ndensity, pin the result in both engines.

  • The reference_words argument of run_pipeline() takes effect. For a corpus or pool design, the pipeline recomputes N and OLD20, and bigram frequency where the lexicon carries it or the design uses it, against the supplied list, overriding the lexicon’s columns, and logs the step. The datasheet’s selection$neighbourhood_reference gains applied_to, the columns recomputed, and is written only when the list was applied. Every bundled lexicon carries N and OLD20, so the argument was ignored while the datasheet recorded it as applied. A generate or table design does not use the argument, and its run log now says that it was ignored. A list that is empty or holds a missing value is refused, since it would set every N to 0 and every OLD20 to missing. A lexicon may mark the forms that make up the neighbourhood reference with a reference_member column of 0 and 1, which load_pool() honours too.

  • The schema documents reference_member and when the derived dimensions are computed, so the committed datasheets, which record its SHA-256, and the run logs, which record the datasheets’ MD5, are regenerated. No stimulus, report table or experiment changes.

  • items.generation.exclude lists further word forms that a generated pseudoword must not equal: files with one form per line, CSV files with a word column, or corpora fetched into the cache with fetch_corpus(). The forms are normalised as a lexicon’s words are, and the datasheet records each list with its checksum as selection$generation_exclude, a field of datasheet format 1.2. The Methods paragraph names the lists. The generators checked only the lexicon, whose English and Spanish forms stop at Zipf 2.95 and 3.11, so real words such as crier and pall, and in Spanish renos and esteras, passed as pseudowords. generate_pseudowords() and build_lexdec_stimuli() take the list as exclude. The repository’s corpora/fetch_corpora.py --known-forms writes wordfreq’s fuller word lists for this purpose (289,023 English and 334,625 Spanish forms), and neither package ships them. No shipped design uses the key yet, so no stimulus moves. The schema’s comments describe it, so the 42 committed datasheets, which record the schema’s SHA-256, and their run logs are regenerated.

  • A generated lexical-decision design reports the number of words the generator could use. It reported the band before the a-z filter, 8,305 words where 6,937 were eligible in a Spanish band of length 4-7 and Zipf 3.5-6. The English demonstrations’ counts do not change, since their bands hold only a-z words.

  • Lexical-decision generation works with accented letters. The generators’ alphabet is the set of letters the reference lexicon attests, in UTF-8 byte order. A Spanish design therefore keeps its accented words, 16.5% of a typical band (1,368 of the 8,305 words of length 4-7 and Zipf 3.5-6, among them 261 preterites in -ó), and can generate accented pseudowords. The generators substituted only the letters a to z and left those words out. A word is now eligible when every character in it is a letter the reference attests, so a word with a hyphen, an apostrophe or a digit is still left out. The subsyllabic segmenter finds its nuclei among accented vowels too, and make_pseudoword() gains an alphabet argument. A word in a logographic script, such as Chinese, is refused with a message. Unicode counts its characters as letters, but a form made by swapping one for another is of unknown validity as a pseudoword. A generated design’s datasheet counts the eligible words, so the Spanish band above now counts all 8,305. A new example, es_lexdec, checks its pseudowords against wordfreq’s Spanish word list. English selections and every other committed output are unchanged. The twin-edge case generation_exclude gains a hyphenated word, which the count leaves out, and its known-form list now names the forms its new selection would otherwise produce. The new case lexdec_logographic pins the refusal in both engines.

  • matching.tie_break chooses how exact ties between equally close candidates are broken. bytes breaks them by spelling, as lexsync 0.1 did, and reproduces its selections. hash breaks them by a keyed SHA-256 of each word (salt lexsync-tie-v1), which favours no part of the alphabet and does not depend on the seed. Ties decide most picks because lengths and neighbourhood counts are whole numbers and frequencies have two decimals. In en_freqcontrast, 71 of the 80 anchored picks had another candidate at the chosen distance, and breaking them by spelling filled conditions with early-alphabet words. In its low-frequency condition, 61% of the words began with a or b, against 13% of the candidates, and in en_ndensity‘s dense condition and the en_andrews_repro low-frequency cells every word did, an initial-letter confound the realised-control report cannot see. Under hash, the low-frequency share fell to 12.5% and the dense share to 17.5%, against 13% and 12% among the candidates, and Cohen’s d on every matched dimension of every shipped matched design was unchanged. The rule decides the anchored picks, the order of tied pairs in joint and optimal matching and the rows tied at their candidate cap. The even spreads that pick the anchor’s items and a continuous design’s items keep the byte order. Under either rule, standardised_euclidean and joint select identical items in the two engines. The datasheet records the rule as selection$tie_break, a 1.2 field, with the salt under hash. Its Markdown no longer says that selection is deterministic given the seed and free of item-selection bias. Selection does not depend on the seed, which fixes the trial order, and the Markdown and the Methods paragraph now say so. The Methods sentence that read ’deterministic and reproducible (seed 2026; lexsync 0.1.1)’ now reads ‘deterministic and reproducible (lexsync 0.1.1), and the seed (2026) fixes the trial order’. The schema gains tie_break, and the twin-edge case tie_hash_small pins the hash rule in both engines.

  • count_syllables() counts the vowels of Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Romanian, Turkish, Danish, Norwegian and Vietnamese (ae, oe, the dotless i and the vowels with an ogonek, caron, breve, macron, ring or double acute), and returns NA for a word in another script, where it returned 0. It now decomposes a word and sets its diacritics aside, so a vowel counts whatever its accent. Every Chinese, Russian or Greek word counted 0 syllables, so a design could match on n_syllables and report perfect balance. run_pipeline() refuses a design that refers to n_syllables when a word without it passes the other filters the lexicon can answer. The documentation said the vowel class covered the Latin-1 vowels, but it lacked ae. The n_syllables column of zh_freqcontrast’s stimuli is now empty, and its datasheets and run logs change with it. No selection changes.

  • Responses are collected from the onset of the stimulus they answer, and every target records them. The response window used to open only when the target had gone, 800 ms after its onset in lexical decision, and each target discarded a key pressed while the target was on screen: jsPsych showed the target with no keys allowed, PsychoPy’s waitKeys() cleared earlier presses and OpenSesame’s keyboard item flushed them. jsPsych timed the reaction from the blank response screen, and the PsychoPy and OpenSesame targets recorded no response at all, so no accuracy, reaction time or reading time reached a data file. The 0.1.0 notes said that a categorisation design’s data were scoreable. That held for jsPsych only. A response event after a text event now opens its window at that stimulus’s onset, for the same total window, and a response ends the trial. from: offset on a response event keeps the delayed window, which is also the default after any other event, and from: onset after such an event is refused. A response collected from the onset runs where its stimulus runs, so a design that gives the two different blocks is refused. The PsychoPy script writes data/<base>_p<participant>_v<version>_<date>-<time>.csv, one row per trial, written as it goes, with the response, its reaction time from the stimulus’s onset, timeouts, accuracy when the item names its answer, self-paced reading times, the question’s response, and each event’s realised flips and onset. The OpenSesame experiment collects the response in the stimulus’s own script, clears the response variables as each trial starts and logs every trial with a logger item. The jsPsych page saves its CSV as before, and its target is now one trial whose rt runs from the onset. The datasheet records each response window as presentation.response_windows, says in analysis.response where a reaction time starts, and its Methods text says when responses were collected. The R engine writes a response key given alone as a list of one key, as the Python engine does. jsonlite wrote it as a bare string, and the PsychoPy runner split that into letters. Every demonstration’s experiments, datasheets and run logs change. No stimulus moves.

  • OpenSesame response and question timeouts are written in whole milliseconds as declared. A timeout of 1,001 ms was written as 1,000, because the value went through seconds and back, and 95 of the whole-millisecond values from 1 to 10,000 came out a millisecond short. The demonstrations’ timeouts were not affected.

  • A screened English lexicon, corpora/derived/en_v2.csv, holds the same 30,000 wordfreq forms as en.csv with columns from SUBTLEX-US (Brysbaert & New, 2009): in_subtlex_us, lowercase_share and nonstandard, which marks forms absent from SUBTLEX-US or beginning with a lower-case letter in under a tenth of their uses (names, acronyms and many internet forms, 6,565 in all). Its N and OLD20 are computed against the 23,435 unmarked forms only, so the marked forms no longer count as neighbours (cat has 21 where en.csv gives 32), and n_density_raw and old20_raw keep the old values. Filter with pool_filters: {nonstandard: [0, 0]}. en.csv is unchanged, so designs that must reproduce earlier selections keep working. The repository’s corpora/fetch_corpora.py --screen-en rebuilds the file byte for byte from a SUBTLEX-US copy whose checksum it verifies, and corpora/ATTRIBUTION.md and LICENSE-DATA credit SUBTLEX-US as its direct source. This is repository data, and the package example slices follow later.

  • A design can exclude words with exclude_words, a list or a file with one word per line, applied before the pool filters and recorded in the datasheet with its checksum. The words are keyed as a lexicon’s are and leave the candidates of a corpus, pool or generated design after the norms join. The neighbourhood reference, and the words a generated pseudoword must not equal, keep them. The datasheet records the list as materials_source$exclusions (its path or inline, checksum, words listed and candidates removed), a field of datasheet format 1.2, the run log notes the removal, and the Methods paragraph reports it. A design with an item table refuses the key. The twin-edge case exclude_words_inline pins both engines to one outcome.

  • The datasheet and the Methods text credit wordfreq only for the lexica lexsync ships. A user’s own lexicon was described as wordfreq data, so a study selecting from SUBTLEX would have cited the wrong corpus. It is now named by its file name and checksum, and a corpus fetched into the cache by the registry’s citation. A shipped lexicon is recognised by its checksum with CRLF line endings read as LF, and the credit for en_v2.csv states its screening rule. The shipped designs’ credits do not change, and the twin-edge case user_lexicon_provenance pins both engines. The schema’s comments describe the new key and columns, so the 42 committed datasheets, which record the schema’s SHA-256, and their run logs are regenerated. No stimulus, report table or experiment changes.

  • The documentation now states what the lexica derived from wordfreq contain: proper names, acronyms and other non-standard forms among the most frequent forms, spread unevenly over frequency bands, with N and OLD20 computed over them. It says that a continuous design spreads items over the predictor’s ranks and not over its range, so the selection follows the pool’s distribution and the tolerance windows trim the controls’ tails without holding them constant, which the 0.1.0 entry for select_continuous_stimuli() misstated. It also says that generated pseudowords are more bigram-typical than their base words, that the priming paradigm is backward-masked, that en_rastle_repro and en_andrews_repro reproduce item selection and not a lexical-decision task, and how each presentation target times its events.

  • The corpus registry no longer maps freq_zipf to the SUBTLEX-US and SUBTLEX-DE log-count columns or to a column that the Chinese SUBTLEX file does not contain. It says that its column maps are not yet applied and that no entry can yet be downloaded by fetch_corpus(), and DESCRIPTION names what the corpus access covers in place of calling it many-language.

  • The documentation of cohens_d_ci() and tost_equiv() cites Sassenhagen and Alday (2016) and Lakens (2017) for what they argue, and calls the 0.5 bound a convention. The quick start in the README and the Get started vignette uses 60 items per condition, as the Python twin’s does, in place of 15: at the default bound and alpha, no dimension that varies can pass the equivalence test with fewer than 23 items per condition. No stimulus, report table or experiment changes. Every JSON datasheet records the new schema digest, the five demonstrations whose design files were corrected record new design digests, and the Markdown datasheets of the four whose descriptions changed (en_andrews_repro, en_freqcontinuous, en_priming_continuous and en_rastle_repro) change with them, as do the run logs.

  • optimal matching minimises the summed distance of the n pairs it selects. It solved a complete assignment over both candidate pools and kept the n cheapest assigned pairs, which is not the optimum and was consistently worse than greedy joint: 1.15 to 2.5 times the optimal summed distance in tests where joint came within 3.4%. It now solves the cardinality-constrained problem exactly with a padded assignment (Volgenant, 2004). In R a problem at the 1,200-candidate cap takes about 4 s, where the complete assignment took 34 s on the same machine. Both capped pools are put in tie-break order before the solve, by spelling under bytes as well as by key under hash, so the solver’s choice among equally cheap pairs no longer depends on the order in which the rows arrive. When the conditions overlap, a word cannot be paired with itself or used twice. A pair the solve loses that way is replaced by solving again over the unused words, and the selection is then no longer guaranteed to have the least summed distance. Designs using optimal select different items, a breaking change under the package’s versioning rule. No shipped design uses it, so no stimulus moves. The schema’s description of the method, corrected in all three copies, changes config/schema.yaml, so every committed datasheet records a new schema digest and every run log a new datasheet checksum.

  • run_pipeline() and run_all() fall back to the schema bundled with the package when none is named and none is found beside the designs, as the Python command line already did, so the one-call pipeline works outside a clone. Both now default to schema_path = NULL. Before the bundled copy, run_pipeline() looks for config/schema.yaml and then for schema.yaml beside the design, and run_all() looks in config_dir and then in config/. The first place each function looks is its old default, so a call that worked before reads the same file. A message names the schema chosen, and the run log (schema_path) and the datasheet (reproducibility$schema_path) record its path, so the choice is visible even when messages are suppressed. Every committed datasheet and run log gains that field. A named schema that does not exist is still an error, and the message gives the bundled copy’s location.

  • The realised-control report covers every dimension lexsync knows for the items, not only the standard four and match_on: syllables, bigram frequency, every joined norm column and every define_by dimension, each with a role (manipulated, controlled or uncontrolled), and it compares every pair of conditions, the anchor rows first. Uncontrolled differences used to go unreported while the Methods text called the control close: in en_ndensity the dense words had fewer estimated syllables than the sparse ones (d = -0.83), and a norm used to define the conditions did not appear in the report at all. Each comparison also gives the raw mean difference in the dimension’s own unit (mean_diff). The comparisons gain rows, and two columns, mean_diff and role, after the existing ones. A dimension is manipulated in a pair whose define_by windows on it differ, so in en_andrews_repro frequency is uncontrolled between the two high-frequency cells. match_report() takes the roles as roles, a function of the condition, reference and dimension that run_pipeline() derives from the design, and leaves out a dimension with no numeric value, such as n_syllables for Chinese. Bigram frequency is computed for the report on a copy of the stimuli, so no stimuli file or selection changes. The datasheet’s realised_control entries gain condition, reference and mean_diff, fields of datasheet format 1.2, and their roles replace ‘manipulated/free’, the label every unmatched dimension was given. Both apps show each row’s role and raw difference and label each bar of the chart by dimension and pair. The comparisons, datasheets and run logs of the eleven demonstrations that match conditions change, and so do the descriptives of all of them but en_richdim, whose report had syllables and bigram frequency already. The twin-edge cases’ pinned reports are regenerated, and the new case four_conditions pins the pairs and roles in both engines.

  • A generated lexical-decision design reports bigram frequency, N and OLD20 for the words against the pseudowords, marked uncontrolled. Its stimuli give the base word of each pseudoword and the edit distance from it, as the base and edit_distance columns build_lexdec_stimuli() now returns. Its pseudowords were more bigram-typical than their words (d about -1.5 in en_lexdec), which no report showed. The reports, datasheets and run logs of the three lexical-decision demonstrations change and their stimuli gain the two columns, while no pseudoword, trial order or experiment changes.

  • A continuous design’s report gives the predictor’s SD against that of as many values spread evenly over its range, each control’s SD against the pool’s, and the control windows (sd, sd_ratio, window_low and window_high). An even spread has a predictor ratio of 1 whatever its size. In en_freqcontinuous, the frequency SD is 0.60 of that of an even spread. select_continuous_stimuli() records the windows and the pool’s SDs as the control_windows entry of its "audit" attribute. match_report_continuous() reads them there, or takes them as audit, and the datasheet’s continuous entries gain the four fields, in datasheet format 1.2. The comparisons, datasheets and run logs of en_freqcontinuous and en_priming_continuous change.

  • cohens_d() and cohens_d_ci() return NA when a condition has fewer than two items, where they returned 0, a perfect balance. The Python pipeline no longer fails while formatting the missing interval. The twin-edge case shortfall_one pins the result in both engines.

  • The Methods text reports the realised control descriptively: the largest difference on a matched dimension, in its own unit and with its pair, d and interval, and then the equivalence tests as a secondary check that says when the number of items is too small for them ever to pass (fewer than 23 per condition at the default bound). It called the control close, or not confirmed, on the tests alone. It names, largest first, up to five comparisons of an uncontrolled dimension that differ by more than the bound, and a generated lexical decision says how its words and pseudowords differ in bigram frequency, N and OLD20. It states the number of items each condition holds, with the request beside it when a shortfall: allow run fell short, where it stated the request. It labels the interval by the configured alpha, where it always said 90%, and for a continuous design it reports the realised spreads, the control windows and any widened window in place of ‘near-constant’. The Markdown table of the realised control gains the pair and the raw difference of each row. The datasheet records the items each condition holds as items$n_per_condition_realised, a field of datasheet format 1.2, and design$n_per_condition gives the request the selector applied, its default when the design gives none, where it was null. The datasheets and run logs of every demonstration change, and no stimulus, report table or experiment does. The twin-edge case shortfall_one pins the new fields.

  • The suggested model uses the stimuli’s condition column, where a lexical decision named a lexicality column the stimuli do not have. It adds a matched design’s matched dimensions as centred covariates on the stimuli file’s own columns (Sassenhagen & Alday, 2016), leaving out one that does not vary among the items. It gives items a random slope for condition whenever the counterbalancing recipe rotates the conditions over the items by a Latin square (the categorisation design had none), crosses the condition with the predictor in a continuous pair design, with by-subject slopes for both and their interaction, and says how to recode a crossed design into its factors. Its note calls the random-effects structure maximal (Barr et al., 2013) only when it is, and describes the slopes of a design whose covariates or controls enter as fixed effects only.

  • Exact ties between equally close candidates are broken by the keyed hash by default (matching.tie_break: hash), and tie_break: bytes reproduces the selections of lexsync 0.1. Every design whose matched dimensions tie selects different items, a breaking change under the package’s versioning rule, and a design or schema that names bytes selects what it did. The schema sets tie_break: hash in all three copies. Of the shipped designs, the Spanish and Chinese ones (es_freqcontrast, es_ndensity, es_gender_repro and zh_freqcontrast) change their stimuli, reports, experiments and datasheets for this reason alone, and the English ones for the change below as well. Four twin-edge cases whose picks ties decided are pinned anew (four_conditions, joint_nan, nfd_pool and user_lexicon_provenance), baseline_small pins the hash rule in its datasheet, and the new case tie_bytes_small holds both engines to the rule of lexsync 0.1.

  • The English demonstrations select from the screened lexicon, corpora/derived/en_v2.csv, with pool_filters: {nonstandard: [0, 0]}, leave out the words of config/exclude_en_demo.txt through exclude_words, and check their generated pseudowords against wordfreq’s fuller English list, corpora/derived/en_known_forms.txt. Every English demonstration that draws its items from a lexicon or a supplied pool selects different items, a breaking change. The selections no longer hold a form the screen marks. The en_andrews_repro low-frequency cells held 24 such forms among their 36 items (aclu, adhd, bbq and bmx among them), where its high-frequency cells held none. The screen lets through taboo words and some forms that are not standard English words, such as abbreviations that subtitles write in lower case (mph, msg, yrs), and the exclusion list leaves them out. Its 53 forms were found by reading the demonstrations’ selections until a run selected none of them, and its header states the criteria. They include the taboo forms the 0.1 demonstrations selected: bitch and boobs in en_ndensity, fuck in en_freqcontrast, ass, damn and hell in en_andrews_repro, and asses and shit in en_resample. The maintainer signs off the list’s content. No generated pseudoword is a known English word now. The check leaves the generators fewer candidates, so more pseudowords are ill-formed at an edge or lack a vowel, as fdes, gngs and ntena do. The matching vignette counts 13 of the 140, against 5 when the same designs skip the check. en_supplied_pool and en_priming_continuous read their norms from en_v2.csv, whose N and OLD20 count only the unmarked forms, so en_supplied_pool selects different words and en_priming_continuous keeps its pairs while its stimuli gain the members’ screening columns. The documentation quotes the new figures. In en_ndensity, the dense words have fewer estimated syllables than the sparse ones by d = -0.53, where the unscreened selection gave -0.83, and in en_lexdec the pseudowords are more bigram-typical than their words by d = -0.97, where they were by -1.47.

  • The English example lexicon, inst/extdata/en_example.csv, holds 3,000 of the forms en_v2.csv keeps, with its frequencies, N and OLD20, and the Python package bundles the same file. It was a slice of en.csv, a quarter of it forms the screen marks, mostly names and acronyms. Examples and tests that use it give different numbers: in the quick start, frequency separates the conditions by d = 4.84, where it gave 5.92. The datasheet credits the slice as screened against SUBTLEX-US, and LICENSE.note and the repository’s LICENSE-DATA credit SUBTLEX-US as a direct source of it. The repository’s corpora/fetch_corpora.py --slice-en rebuilds it from the committed en_v2.csv, as --screen-en now does too. The script writes the slices with LF line ends on every platform, and rebuilding en.csv no longer overwrites the English slice.

  • Lexica that the Python package’s wordfreq connector builds for Hindi, Bengali, Persian, Ukrainian and Catalan now hold the words those languages spell with combining marks, a zero-width non-joiner, an apostrophe or a middle dot. The connector dropped them, so a Hindi lexicon of 10,000 forms came back with 3,207, most of them Latin-script tokens such as ‘and’. The R package reads the new lexica as before and, like the Python package, counts their length, N and OLD20 in code points.

  • Durations that resolve_trial_timing() reads from an item column must be present, finite and not negative. Fractional milliseconds are rounded once and recorded. A blank or negative value used to produce experiments that stopped at the blank in OpenSesame and PsychoPy or showed the stimulus for no time in jsPsych. A fractional one made the R and Python jsPsych pages differ, because jsonlite kept four decimal places of it. A blank, negative or non-numeric value is now refused, naming the column and the trial’s set and condition. A column of fractional milliseconds is rounded with the rounder both engines share and written back to the stimuli and the loop tables, so 82.5 ms is presented as 83 in every target. The returned table records how many values were rounded in its "duration_rounding" attribute, and run_pipeline() writes the count into the run log. Fixed durations are checked the same way. A negative duration_ms, duration_frames or timing value reached OpenSesame as clock.sleep(-50), and a NaN as clock.sleep(NA), and both are now refused, naming the event or the key. A fractional duration_ms is rounded where it was truncated, so 33.7 ms is presented as 34, and the lower bound of a jitter must not be negative. The jsPsych page writes each trial’s numbers to 15 significant digits, as the Python engine does. No shipped design reads a fractional or blank duration, so no stimulus or experiment changes. The twin-edge case fractional_soa pins both engines to one outcome.

  • Trigger codes are checked when the experiment is generated. A literal must be a whole number from 1 to 255, written as a number or as a string of digits, and anything else is refused with a message naming the event. A misspelt token such as conditon was written into the OpenSesame experiment as send_trigger(NA), while the Python engine stopped. Codes such as 300, 0 and -5 reached the parallel port, which keeps only the low byte, and 20.5 was taken as 20. A literal of 254 or 255, which the PsychoPy experiment sends when the session starts and ends, is reported, and so is one equal to a condition code the design sends or one within the range of the item codes it sends. A design that sends item codes together with condition codes, or with a code of its own from 40 to 239, gets item codes that never coincide with those codes. Sets 65 and 66 of a 70-set design took 101 and 102, the condition codes. Such a design is refused before any file is written when it has more item sets than free codes, unless the schema sets the new triggers.allow_code_overlap: true, which lets the item codes wrap and repeat within the free codes. assign_triggers() gains events and schema arguments for this, and export_experiments() passes them. Any other design keeps its item codes, so no shipped loop table changes. The experiments vignette now says that item codes follow the code-point order of the set labels, so that with sets 1 to 20 set 10 is 41 and set 2 is 51, and that they are decoded through the loop table. It said that condition codes stay unique regardless. The codes did, but the marker stream did not once both kinds were sent. The OpenSesame snippet inline_send_triggers.py sends only the condition code at the word’s onset. It sent the item code first, whose 10 ms pulse delayed the condition code. The schema’s comments describe the new key, so the 42 committed datasheets, which record the schema’s SHA-256, and their run logs are regenerated. No stimulus, report table or experiment changes. The twin-edge case trigger_typo pins the refusal in both engines.

  • Generated OpenSesame experiments build every stimulus before the trial runs and time each event from its onset. Each inline script built its canvas while the trial ran and slept the event’s full duration after a trigger pulse that blocked for 10 ms, the pattern OpenSesame’s timing manual shows as the way not to time a display, so every event overran: at 60 Hz the 50 ms prime was predicted to last about 67 ms and the 83 ms stimulus-onset asynchrony from prime to target about 117 ms. Each event now ends half a frame before its duration is up, so that the next display lands on the refresh that ends it. On a simulated display at 60, 120 and 144 Hz, the prime and the mask then last the flips the PsychoPy script gives them, and the asynchrony stays 83.3 ms. These figures are predictions, and the experiments vignette now gives a photodiode checklist for measuring them. The experiment measures the display’s frame period at start-up and logs it as lexsync_frame_ms. It holds each trigger code for trigger_hold_ms, which it ignored, without delaying any display. A response kept after the stimulus with from: offset opens its window once a code still held has been reset, since OpenSesame’s keyboard_response runs none of lexsync’s code. The experiment also sends the 254 and 255 session markers, as the PsychoPy script does. The 32 committed .osexp files change, and so do the datasheets and run logs that record their checksums. No stimulus moves.

  • Trigger codes in the PsychoPy script last the hold, and never less than 10 ms. The 254 and 255 session markers were cleared by the statement after their flip, and a code on an event shorter than the hold was cleared as soon as the event’s last flip returned, so the markers and a one-flip prime’s code lasted no time at all. A hold set to 10 ms was rounded to 6.9 ms at 144 Hz and 8.3 ms at 240 Hz. The default 50 ms hold was not affected. Every code is now counted down flip by flip and reset on the flip that ends its hold, in a later event when its own is shorter. Only the next onset’s code ends it sooner, and a key that ends a stimulus early no longer cuts its code short. The self-paced reading critical-region code is held the same way. It was held for inter_trigger_ms, 10 ms, which is accepted and no longer used: validate_design() returns a note for the run log when a schema sets it, and the shipped schema no longer does. A literal code of 254 or 255 is reported as a code both laboratory targets send. The 21 committed PsychoPy scripts change, and the datasheets and run logs are regenerated. No stimulus moves.

  • The generated PsychoPy experiment runs full screen (presentation.fullscreen, true by default), as PsychoPy advises for frame timing. It always ran in a 1280 x 1024 window, which fullscreen: false keeps. Text is 48 pixels high in all three targets (presentation.text_height_px, a whole number from 8 to 400), where the OpenSesame experiment used 32. In OpenSesame, the setting is the experiment’s font_size, so its instructions grow with it. OpenSesame takes full screen from the mode it is launched in, as the experiments vignette now says. Every committed experiment changes, and so do the datasheets and run logs, which record the checksums of the experiments and the schema. No stimulus moves.

  • triggers.mode (auto, hardware or mock) decides what the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments do when the trigger device cannot be opened. hardware refuses to start: the PsychoPy script stops before its window opens, and the OpenSesame experiment stops in its setup. auto, the default, falls back to printing the codes as before, but now says so on screen before the first trial, where the experimenter presses C to go on, and records the mode with every trial, as trigger_mode in the PsychoPy data file and as lexsync_trigger_mode in the OpenSesame log. Both experiments used to run on without triggers and with no notice on screen, and only the OpenSesame log said so, in its test_mode column. mock prints the codes without trying the device, after the same notice. triggers.backend: serial, with triggers.serial_port and triggers.baudrate (115200 by default), sends each code as one byte over a serial port in both experiments. The OpenSesame setup had a serial branch that ran only once the script was edited by hand, and it then opened the first serial port it found. The OpenSesame snippet inline_trigger_setup.py took the first serial port too, and now opens the one named at its top. validate_design() refuses a serial backend without a port, a port name that cannot be written into the experiments, a mode or backend lexsync does not know, and a baud rate, text height or full-screen setting of the wrong kind, before anything is written. The experiments vignette describes the delay a USB-serial adapter adds. The twin-edge case trigger_serial pins both engines to one outcome.

  • The jsPsych page loads jsPsych, its keyboard plugin and its stylesheet from unpkg with Subresource Integrity, each file’s SHA-384 and crossorigin="anonymous", so a browser refuses a modified copy. The page loaded them with no integrity check, and the first two from bare package addresses that the CDN answers with a redirect. The page’s comment says how to run it offline, since a page opened from a file:// address cannot check the hash of a local copy.

lexsync 0.1.1

CRAN release: 2026-09-25

  • assign_triggers() gains a conditions argument that fixes the order of the condition codes, and export_experiments() gains one that defaults to the order of the design’s conditions. The codes used to follow the order in which the conditions first appeared in the counterbalanced trials, so a different seed could swap them, and low_frequency was 101 in a design that lists high_frequency first. The pipeline now passes the design’s order, followed by any other condition in the order the item source lists it, so the first condition the design lists is 101. The condition codes of 12 of the 21 demonstration designs change with it. assign_triggers() called without conditions behaves as before.
  • cohens_d_ci() uses the large-sample standard error of d, sqrt(1/nx + 1/ny + d^2 / (2 * (nx + ny))) (Hedges & Olkin, 1985; Borenstein et al., 2009). It left out the d^2 term, which treated the pooled SD as known and made the interval on a manipulated dimension far too narrow. In the English frequency contrast, d = 5.27 had the interval [5.01, 5.53] and now has [4.72, 5.83]. A matched control, whose d is near zero, moves by at most 0.002 across the 21 demonstration designs, and no d, TOST p-value or verdict changes. The comparisons, datasheets and run logs of the designs with a manipulated dimension change with it. No stimulus moves.
  • match_report() documents the direction of its signed statistics. cohens_d and its interval are the reference (first) condition’s mean minus the mean of the condition in that row, and var_ratio is that condition’s variance over the reference’s.
  • New lexsync_cache_clear() removes a fetched corpus from the cache, together with any partial download of it, or with no argument removes the whole cache. It returns the paths it removed, invisibly.
  • lexsync_cache_dir() only reports the cache’s path. It created the directory on every call, so asking where the cache was left an empty directory behind. fetch_corpus() now creates the cache when a download into it starts, once the registry entry and its URL have been accepted, so a refused call writes nothing. That download begins by deleting any .part sidecar in the cache that has gone a day without a write. An interrupt or a process that died mid-transfer leaves one behind, and no handler removes it. A younger sidecar may belong to a download still running in another session, so it is left alone. A dest of the caller’s choosing behaves as before.
  • citation("lexsync") gives the DOI that CRAN assigned to the package, https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.lexsync, with the CRAN page as its URL. The 0.1.0 build on CRAN predates the DOI and gives the repository’s address. The entry names CRAN as its publisher, and its text version is the APA reference for software: author, year, title, version, “[Computer software]”, CRAN and the DOI.
  • The tests no longer take another package’s sources for the lexsync repository. CRAN’s Linux hosts check each package beside the unpacked sources of the others, and the test holding the bundled templates to the repository’s templates/ directory found the unrelated ‘templates’ package there and failed. A test that compares the package with repository files now accepts a root only if it holds lexsync’s own DESCRIPTION under R_workflow/ and the Python package beside it, and skips on CRAN.
  • Suggests now asks for testthat 3.1.8, the first release whose local_mocked_bindings() can replace an imported function, as the corpus download tests do with download.file().

lexsync 0.1.0

CRAN release: 2026-09-22

  • First release: multilingual corpus access, parallel multidimensional matching, counterbalancing, item resampling, deterministic pseudoword generation, and generation of hardware-timed PsychoPy, OpenSesame and jsPsych experiments. The R and Python engines select byte-identical stimuli, and every run ships a materials datasheet (provenance, checksums, realised control) and a pre-registration template.
  • See the top-level CHANGELOG.md for the full, cross-language history and the planned methodological roadmap.

Changes made before the release

These notes follow the package through its development up to the release, so they describe each change against the state it replaced.

  • The package now declares Depends: R (>= 4.0.0). tools::R_user_dir does not exist before 4.0.0, and round()’s post-4.0 algorithm shapes artefact bytes, so an older R would fail obscurely or write different bytes without complaint.
  • The published median goes through the exact reductions. describe_stimuli() was the one reduction still on stats::median, which averages the two middle values through mean()’s long-double accumulator while the Python engine reduced through numpy. Both engines now sort and take the exact middle, with (a + b) / 2 in plain double arithmetic for even n, and regenerating every design moved no byte. Reproducibility and parity claimed that every reduction shared one compensated-summation algorithm, which the median never did, and now describes the sort-and-middle rule beside it.
  • The dead half of the two-shortest-forms CSV guard now fires. Between 2^49 and 1e15 two one-decimal strings can round-trip to the same double, and the R check derived its digit count from a 15-digit format that never shows a fractional digit there, so R accepted values (844424930131968.2 among them) that the Python writer refused. R now refuses exactly the same values, and the change only adds refusals.
  • A condition without define_by selects identically in both engines. This engine always fell back to the whole pool. The Python engine crashed with a bare KeyError on the same design and now mirrors the fallback, pinned by twin tests.
  • A pair design’s tolerance-window relaxation reaches the run log and datasheet. The continuous-pairs selector’s re-expansion dropped the audit in both engines, so a relaxed window left no trace outside the console. No shipped pair design relaxes, so no committed artefact changed.
  • INTER_TRIGGER_S is substituted through %.17g like its neighbours in the generated PsychoPy script. It used as.character(), whose rendering of a non-integer quotient differs from Python’s str(). The shipped default still renders “0.01”, so no committed experiment byte moved.
  • The counterbalancing hash keys convert to UTF-8 before hashing, as hash_unit() always has, so a latin1-marked condition read from a user’s CSV can no longer rank by different digests in the two engines.
  • The command-line wrapper reports which copy of the package it loaded. R_workflow/run_pipeline.R prefers an installed lexsync over the edited sources, so edits silently did nothing until a reinstall. It now states the loaded copy and the remedy on stderr at startup.
  • The Shiny app writes its design YAML with LF endings through a binary connection (the datasheet hashes that file into design_sha256, which must not depend on the operating system), and its parity caption now matches the keyed-hash guarantee: the engines produce byte-identical stimuli and trial order, where the caption used to promise only the stimuli. The Python engine’s twin fixes land in the same release: its writer refuses 16-digit integer columns as this engine always has, its scalar rounder passes an overflowing scale through, and run_pipeline(verbose = FALSE) keeps its console silent.
  • A selection that cannot honour n_per_condition is now an error. Every selector used to clip the request to the available pool and said so at most through a verbose message, while the datasheet and the generated Methods text kept stating the requested n. The new matching: shortfall policy defaults to error, and allow accepts the shrink. Its sibling matching: on_insufficient_tolerance (default relax) can likewise turn the silent tolerance-window widening into a refusal, and a relaxation that does happen is now recorded in the run log and the datasheet (selection.window_relaxations), where before it was only narrated to the console. No committed design experiences either condition.
  • joint and optimal matching can no longer select the same word twice. With overlapping condition windows a word could be paired with itself at zero cost, or mirrored across two sets, appearing in both conditions.
